patient.name: Desmond Clarke
patient.complaint: Right groin lump that comes and goes for 4 months
background: Scaffolder in Lewisham; lifts heavy loads daily
Smoker, 30 pack-years, with a chronic morning cough
No previous abdominal surgery; no regular medicines

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a groin lump: the pubic tubercle decides inguinal versus femoral, the deep ring test decides indirect versus direct, and tenderness with colour change means strangulation.

points: Desmond, 58, has a **right groin lump** for 4 months.
Bigger at the end of a shift and when he coughs.
Disappears when he lies down; a **dragging ache** on lifting.
No vomiting, bowels normal, no scrotal swelling.

visual.title: Where Desmond's lump is
visual.caption: The right groin, just above the inguinal ligament. Next step: find the pubic tubercle.

steps.lead: Desmond's lump is abdominal contents pushing through a weak spot. The first question is always **inguinal or femoral**.
**Male**, heavy lifting, a smoker's cough and constipation: every one raises Desmond's **intra-abdominal pressure**.

points: Standing: a 4 cm soft swelling with a **cough impulse**.
It **reduces** easily when he lies flat.
It sits **above and medial to the pubic tubercle**.
You can get above it; it does not enter the scrotum.

steps.lead: A groin lump, worse on standing and coughing, **reducible** with a cough impulse: Desmond's story is a textbook hernia.

steps.q: Desmond's lump is above and medial to the pubic tubercle. Which hernia is it?
steps.r: Above and medial to the pubic tubercle = **inguinal**. Femoral hernias sit below the ligament, inferolateral to the tubercle.

points: The lump is reduced while he lies flat.
Firm pressure is held over the **deep inguinal ring**.
He stands and coughs: the lump **reappears**, medially.
Pressure on the deep ring does not control it.

steps.lead: Not controlled by deep ring pressure, in an older man with a chronic cough: Desmond has a **direct inguinal hernia** through Hesselbach's triangle.

Direct

steps.lead: Desmond's lump is a groin hernia, but the exam also tests these rarer hernias, each by one signature clue.
Desmond is warned: if the lump becomes **irreducible, tender, red or hot**, or he vomits, it may be **strangulated**.

steps.text: A tender, irreducible lump with **normal bowels** can still be strangulated: a **Richter's hernia** traps only part of the bowel wall, so there is no obstruction.

steps.q: Desmond's lump is easy to feel and reduce. What confirms the diagnosis?

Desmond notices **numbness over his upper inner thigh**.

steps.lead: Desmond's lifting and coughing push a **peritoneal sac** through a weak area of his abdominal wall.

steps.title: From weak wall to emergency
nodes: Peritoneal sac protrudes, with or without contents
Contents stuck in the sac → incarcerated

steps.lead: Desmond's hernia is **acquired**: it pushes straight through the weak posterior wall, **medial** to the inferior epigastric vessels.

steps.q: Desmond's hernia lies medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Through which area does it pass?
steps.r: **Direct** hernias pass through **Hesselbach's triangle**, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Indirect hernias enter the deep ring, lateral to them.

steps.text: **Hesselbach's triangle**: inferior epigastric vessels (lateral), lateral border of rectus abdominis (medial), inguinal ligament (inferior).

steps.lead: If Desmond were a 75 year old woman with a lump below the ligament, the **narrow, rigid femoral canal** would make strangulation far likelier.
A trapped loop in Desmond's hernia would lose its **venous** drainage first, then its **arterial** supply.

nodes: Bowel trapped at a tight neck
steps.caption: Which is why colour change, heat and tenderness are surgical emergencies.

mcq.q: Where does an inguinal hernia lie relative to the pubic tubercle?
mcq.r: Inguinal = **superior and medial**; femoral = inferior and lateral.

mcq.q: Which hernia is typical in an older woman and has a higher strangulation risk?
mcq.r: **Femoral** hernias are commoner in older women and strangulate more often.

mcq.q: Which type of inguinal hernia do children have?
mcq.r: Children's inguinal hernias are always **indirect** (patent processus vaginalis), more on the right and in boys.

mcq.q: Which hernia strangulates without causing bowel obstruction?
mcq.r: In a **Richter's hernia** only part of the bowel wall is trapped.

mcq.q: A tender mass felt per rectum in an elderly woman suggests which hernia?
mcq.r: **Obturator hernia**: tender mass on rectal examination.

mcq.q: Which is the gold-standard diagnosis of a groin hernia?
mcq.r: Hernias are a **clinical diagnosis**; ultrasound if uncertain.

mcq.q: How quickly should a femoral hernia be referred, even if asymptomatic?
mcq.r: **Within 2 weeks**, because of the high strangulation risk.

mcq.q: Which repair suits bilateral or recurrent inguinal hernias?
mcq.r: **Laparoscopic mesh repair** for bilateral or recurrent hernias.

mcq.q: By what age do most small umbilical hernias in babies resolve?
mcq.r: Most resolve by **12 months**; repair at 4 to 5 years if they persist.

mcq.q: An indirect inguinal hernia enters the canal at which point relative to the inferior epigastric vessels?
mcq.r: Indirect hernias enter the **deep ring, lateral** to the inferior epigastric vessels.

prompts.q: What is a hernia, what are the common types, and what raises the risk?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: anything that raises intra-abdominal pressure is a risk factor.

points.p: Protrusion of abdominal contents through a weakness or defect in the wall
points.why: The sac is peritoneum, with or without bowel or omentum.

points.p: Types: inguinal, femoral, umbilical, incisional
Male sex (inguinal); older women (femoral)
points.why: Sex points you to the type.

points.p: Raised intra-abdominal pressure: lifting, chronic cough, constipation, obesity, pregnancy, previous surgery
points.why: Look for the smoker, the constipated or the pregnant patient.

prompts.q: How does a groin hernia present on history and examination?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: reducible + cough impulse = hernia; transillumination = hydrocele.

points.p: Groin lump or dragging sensation, bigger on standing or coughing
Discomfort or pain on standing or lifting
Reducible swelling
Cough impulse
points.why: A hydrocele or varicocele does not reduce like this.

prompts.q: How do you tell an inguinal from a femoral hernia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: find the pubic tubercle in the stem.

points.p: Inguinal: superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
Femoral: below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle
Femoral has a higher strangulation risk
Scrotal lump you cannot get above suggests inguinoscrotal hernia
points.why: A testicular lump you can get above is not a hernia.

prompts.q: How do you tell a direct from an indirect inguinal hernia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the deep ring test, then the epigastric vessels.

points.p: Direct: through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to inferior epigastric vessels
Indirect: patent processus vaginalis, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels
Indirect is controlled by pressure over the deep inguinal ring
points.why: A direct hernia reappears despite pressure.

points.p: Children: always indirect, boys, right side, bulge on crying
points.why: Paediatric repair timings depend on age.

prompts.q: Name the other hernias and the one clue for each: umbilical, incisional, Spigelian, obturator, diaphragmatic, Richter's.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: each rare hernia is tested by a single signature clue.

points.p: Umbilical: infants, obesity, pregnancy; low incarceration risk
points.why: Most in babies close by 12 months.

points.p: Incisional: at a previous surgical scar; Spigelian: through the linea semilunaris
points.why: Spigelian sits at the lateral edge of rectus.

points.p: Obturator: tender mass per rectum
Diaphragmatic: bowel sounds in the chest of a neonate in respiratory distress
Richter's: strangulation without obstruction (part of bowel wall)
points.why: Bowels can be normal despite gangrene.

prompts.q: How do you recognise an incarcerated versus a strangulated hernia?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tenderness, colour change and heat mean the blood supply is going.

points.p: Incarcerated: irreducible, may be tender or red, retains cough impulse
points.why: High risk of progressing to strangulation.

points.p: Strangulated: colour change, irreducible, tender, raised local temperature
Preceding intermittent pain that resolves; obstructive bowel sounds
points.why: Look for vomiting and distension too.

prompts.q: How is a hernia diagnosed, and when is imaging needed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: 'clinical diagnosis' is a real exam answer.

points.p: Gold standard: clinical diagnosis by history and examination
points.why: No imaging for an obvious hernia.

points.p: Indirect: does not reappear on coughing with the deep ring occluded
points.why: The bedside test that types the hernia.

points.p: Ultrasound if the diagnosis is uncertain
points.why: E.g. obese patient or impalpable lump.

prompts.q: How is an uncomplicated inguinal hernia managed, and which repair is used when?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: symptoms, laterality and complication decide the operation.

points.p: Small asymptomatic: watchful waiting with safety-netting
Unilateral uncomplicated: elective open mesh repair
Bilateral or recurrent: laparoscopic mesh repair
Irreducible or strangulated: open non-mesh repair
points.why: Mesh is avoided in a contaminated field.

points.p: Risk: ilioinguinal nerve injury (numb superomedial thigh, base of penis, anterior scrotum/labia)

prompts.q: How is a complicated hernia managed, and what are the timings for femoral, paediatric and umbilical hernias?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: femoral means urgent even when painless.

points.p: Irreducible/strangulated: urgent surgical review or emergency surgery; no manual reduction
Femoral: urgent referral within 2 weeks even without complications
Congenital inguinal: under 6 weeks within 2 days; under 6 months within 2 weeks; under 6 years within 2 months
Umbilical in babies: most resolve by 12 months; repair at 4–5 years if persists (2–3 years if large/symptomatic)
High surgical risk: truss with referral if no improvement; epigastric: weight loss advice
points.why: For the frail patient with short life expectancy.

prompts.q: Why do direct and indirect inguinal hernias differ, and why do femoral hernias strangulate more?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: name the embryological path and the canal.

points.p: Indirect follows the processus vaginalis through the deep ring, lateral to inferior epigastric vessels
points.why: So it can reach the scrotum.

points.p: Direct pushes through the weak posterior wall (Hesselbach's triangle), medial to the vessels
Femoral passes through the narrow, rigid femoral canal

prompts.q: Why does strangulation happen and what does it lead to?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: veins close before arteries.

points.p: Blood supply compromised: venous first, then arterial
points.why: Venous congestion causes swelling that tightens the neck.

points.p: Ischaemia and necrosis
points.why: Explains colour change, heat and tenderness.

points.p: Potential perforation: surgical emergency

glossary.hernia: Protrusion of a structure, usually bowel or fat, through a weakness in the wall that normally contains it.
glossary.inguinal hernia: A hernia through the inguinal canal, above and medial to the pubic tubercle.
glossary.femoral hernia: A hernia through the femoral canal, below the inguinal ligament and inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.
glossary.direct inguinal hernia: Pushes straight through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels.
glossary.indirect inguinal hernia: Enters the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, along a patent processus vaginalis.
glossary.pubic tubercle: The bony bump at the inner end of the inguinal ligament; the key landmark for groin lumps.
glossary.inguinal ligament: The band running from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle.
glossary.deep inguinal ring: The internal opening of the inguinal canal, just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament.
glossary.inguinal canal: A passage through the lower abdominal wall carrying the spermatic cord or round ligament.
glossary.Hesselbach's triangle: Weak area of the posterior inguinal wall bounded by inferior epigastric vessels, rectus and inguinal ligament.
glossary.inferior epigastric vessels: Artery and vein in the lower abdominal wall; the landmark separating direct from indirect hernias.
glossary.processus vaginalis: A fold of peritoneum that follows the testis into the scrotum; if it stays open, an indirect hernia can form.
glossary.femoral canal: A small, narrow, rigid space medial to the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament.
glossary.cough impulse: A palpable expansion of a lump when the patient coughs, typical of a hernia.
glossary.reducible: Can be pushed back into the abdomen.
glossary.irreducible: Cannot be pushed back into the abdomen.
glossary.incarcerated: A hernia that is stuck and irreducible but still has its blood supply.
glossary.strangulated: A hernia whose blood supply is cut off, causing ischaemia; a surgical emergency.
glossary.Richter's hernia: Only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate without causing obstruction.
glossary.obturator hernia: A hernia through the obturator canal of the pelvis; may be felt as a tender mass on rectal examination.
glossary.Spigelian hernia: A hernia through the linea semilunaris at the lateral edge of the rectus sheath.
glossary.linea semilunaris: The curved line along the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle.
glossary.incisional hernia: A hernia through the scar of a previous operation.
glossary.umbilical hernia: A hernia at the umbilicus; common in babies and usually closes by 12 months.
glossary.epigastric hernia: A hernia through the linea alba above the umbilicus.
glossary.diaphragmatic hernia: Abdominal contents pass into the chest through a diaphragm defect; in neonates causes respiratory distress.
glossary.uncal herniation: Brain herniation of the uncus that compresses CN III and causes a dilated pupil.
glossary.inguinoscrotal: A hernia that has travelled down the inguinal canal into the scrotum.
glossary.herniotomy: Operation that removes the hernial sac alone; the standard repair in children.
glossary.mesh repair: Hernia repair using a synthetic mesh to reinforce the weak wall.
glossary.laparoscopic: Keyhole surgery using a camera through small incisions.
glossary.truss: A support belt that holds a reducible hernia in place.
glossary.ilioinguinal nerve: Nerve running in the inguinal canal; injury numbs the upper inner thigh, base of penis and anterior scrotum or labia.
glossary.watchful waiting: Monitoring without surgery, with advice on symptoms that need urgent review.
glossary.ASIS: Anterior superior iliac spine: the bony point at the front of the hip.
glossary.hydrocele: Fluid around the testis; transilluminates and is not reducible.
glossary.varicocele: Dilated veins of the spermatic cord; feels like a 'bag of worms'.

technique.stem: A 3 month old boy is brought by his mother with an intermittent swelling in his right groin. It appears when he cries and disappears when he is asleep. On examination there is a soft swelling lateral to the pubic tubercle with an impulse on crying. It reduces easily. He is feeding well and his abdomen is soft.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A groin lump in a baby: in children, the type of hernia is almost always decided by age alone.
A boy, right side, reducible bulge on crying: a congenital hernia along a patent processus vaginalis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Children's inguinal hernias are **always indirect**.

elim: Direct hernias are acquired in older adults.
Femoral hernias are rare in infants and lie below the ligament.
A hydrocele transilluminates and has no impulse on crying.
An umbilical hernia sits at the umbilicus, not the groin.

steps.x: **D. Indirect inguinal hernia.** Then repair within 2 weeks (under 6 months).

technique.stem: A 52 year old man has a 3 month history of a lump in his right groin that enlarges when he lifts. On standing there is a 3 cm soft swelling superior and medial to the pubic tubercle with a cough impulse. It reduces easily when he lies down. There is no tenderness. The testes are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: What confirms a hernia that is easy to feel?

clues: superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
steps.x: Classic, palpable, reducible inguinal hernia: no doubt clinically.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hernias are a **clinical diagnosis**: history and examination are the gold standard.

elim: CT is for complications such as obstruction, not an obvious hernia.
Herniography is invasive and outdated.
MRI is for occult groin pain, not a clear hernia.
Ultrasound is for an uncertain diagnosis; this one is certain.

steps.x: **A. Clinical examination alone.** Rule: image only when you cannot be sure.

technique.stem: A 67 year old man with a known right inguinal hernia has 6 hours of severe groin pain and vomiting. The swelling is now irreducible, red, hot and very tender. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. His abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management?

steps.x: Management of an acutely painful hernia: first decide if it is strangulated.

clues: irreducible, red, hot and very tender
steps.x: Colour change, heat, tenderness, obstruction and a raised lactate: strangulated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Emergency surgery** (open, usually non-mesh) after resuscitation.

elim: Elective repair is far too slow for dying bowel.
Manual reduction of a strangulated hernia is not recommended.
A truss is for frail patients with reducible hernias.
Waiting risks necrosis and perforation.

steps.x: **B. Emergency surgical repair.** Rule: strangulated = theatre, never push it back.

technique.stem: A 48 year old man has an elective open mesh repair of a left inguinal hernia. Three weeks later he has numbness and tingling over the upper inner part of his left thigh, the base of his penis and the front of his scrotum. The wound has healed well. Hip flexion and knee extension are normal.
technique.q: Which nerve is most likely to have been injured?

steps.x: Applied anatomy: match the numb area to the nerve in the operative field.

clues: upper inner part of his left thigh
steps.x: Sensory loss in the classic ilioinguinal distribution; no motor loss.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **ilioinguinal nerve** runs in the inguinal canal and is at risk in open repair.

elim: Femoral injury weakens knee extension; that is normal.
Genitofemoral gives a small patch of anterior thigh and the cremaster.
Iliohypogastric supplies the suprapubic skin.
Obturator supplies the medial thigh and hip adductors, not the penis.

steps.x: **D. Ilioinguinal nerve.** Rule: thigh + base of penis + anterior scrotum = ilioinguinal.

practice.stem: A 74 year old woman has a 2 month history of a lump in her right groin. It gets bigger when she coughs. There is a 2 cm swelling below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle. It is not tender. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 142/84 mmHg. There is no pulsation and no lymphadenopathy elsewhere.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A lump below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle, enlarging on coughing in an older woman is a femoral hernia. Inguinal hernias are superomedial to the tubercle.

steps.x: Groin lump diagnosis: locate it against the pubic tubercle.

clues: below the inguinal ligament, inferolateral to the pubic tubercle
steps.x: Older woman, below the ligament, enlarges with coughing, not pulsatile.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Femoral hernia.**

elim: An aneurysm is pulsatile and expansile.
Inguinal hernias lie above and medial to the tubercle.
Nodes do not enlarge with coughing.
A saphena varix has a cough thrill and blue tinge, and vanishes lying flat.

steps.x: **B. Femoral hernia.** Then refer urgently within 2 weeks.

practice.stem: A 24 year old man has a swelling in his right groin that extends into his scrotum when he plays football. On standing the examiner cannot get above the scrotal swelling. It does not transilluminate. It reduces lying down, and firm pressure over the deep inguinal ring stops it reappearing when he coughs.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A young man's inguinoscrotal hernia controlled by deep ring pressure is indirect. A direct hernia reappears despite deep ring occlusion and rarely reaches the scrotum.

steps.x: Groin and scrotal lump: hernia or testicular? Then direct or indirect?

clues: cannot get above the scrotal swelling
stops it reappearing when he coughs
steps.x: Cannot get above = inguinoscrotal hernia; controlled at the deep ring = indirect.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Indirect inguinal hernia.**

elim: Direct hernias are not controlled by deep ring pressure.
A hydrocele transilluminates and you can get above it.
A tumour is a hard testicular lump you can get above.
A varicocele is a bag of worms above the testis.

steps.x: **C. Indirect inguinal hernia.** Rule: controlled at deep ring = indirect.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man with COPD and a chronic cough has a lump in his left groin for a year. On standing there is a broad swelling superior and medial to the pubic tubercle with a cough impulse. After reduction, pressure over the deep inguinal ring does not stop the lump reappearing medially when he coughs. It does not enter the scrotum.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: An older man's inguinal hernia that reappears despite deep ring occlusion, medial and not scrotal, is direct (through Hesselbach's triangle). An indirect hernia would be controlled.

steps.x: Diagnosis: which type of groin hernia?

clues: superior and medial to the pubic tubercle
does not stop the lump reappearing medially
steps.x: Inguinal by position; not controlled at the deep ring; older man with raised pressure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Direct inguinal hernia.**

elim: Femoral lies below and lateral to the tubercle.
Indirect is controlled by deep ring pressure.
Spigelian lies at the lateral edge of rectus, higher up.
Umbilical hernias are at the umbilicus.

steps.x: **A. Direct inguinal hernia.** Rule: older + reappears despite deep ring = direct.

practice.stem: A 69 year old man with a known right inguinal hernia has an 8 hour history of severe pain in the lump and vomiting. The lump is irreducible, tense, red and warm. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. His abdomen is distended with tinkling bowel sounds.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Colour change, raised local temperature, tenderness, obstruction and a raised lactate mean the hernia is strangulated. Incarceration alone does not cause redness, heat and a lactate rise.

steps.x: A complicated hernia: incarcerated or strangulated?
Irreducible plus colour change and heat, obstruction, tachycardia and lactate 3.8.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Strangulated inguinal hernia.**

elim: Epididymo-orchitis is a tender testis, without obstruction.
Ischaemic signs and a raised lactate go beyond incarceration.
Nodes do not cause bowel obstruction.
Torsion is a testicular emergency in younger males, no obstruction.

steps.x: **D. Strangulated inguinal hernia.** Next: emergency surgery.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman has a 1 day history of a painful lump in her left groin below the inguinal ligament. The lump is irreducible, tender and red. She is opening her bowels normally and passing flatus. She has not vomited and her abdomen is not distended. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A strangulated-looking hernia (red, tender, irreducible, raised lactate) with normal bowel function is a Richter's hernia, where only part of the bowel wall is trapped; femoral hernias are a classic site.

steps.x: Strangulation signs but no obstruction: which hernia does that?

clues: opening her bowels normally and passing flatus
steps.x: Femoral position, ischaemic lump, but the lumen is not blocked.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Part of the bowel wall is strangulated: **Richter's hernia**.

elim: Obturator hernias are felt per rectum, not as a groin lump.
The lump is irreducible and ischaemic, not reducible.
A saphena varix is soft, compressible and not red.
A Spigelian hernia lies at the edge of rectus, above the groin.

steps.x: **C. Richter's hernia.** Rule: strangulation without obstruction = Richter's.

practice.stem: An 82 year old thin woman has 2 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. She has pain down the inside of her right thigh to the knee. There is no groin lump. A tender mass is felt on the right on rectal examination. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 126/72 mmHg. Bowel sounds are tinkling.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Small bowel obstruction with no groin lump, medial thigh pain and a tender mass per rectum in a thin elderly woman is an obturator hernia.

steps.x: Obstruction with no visible hernia: look for the hidden one.

clues: pain down the inside of her right thigh
tender mass is felt on the right on rectal examination
steps.x: Obturator nerve pain down the medial thigh and a mass per rectum.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Obturator hernia.**

elim: A femoral hernia would be a lump in the groin.
Richter's does not cause obstruction.
Volvulus gives huge distension, not a rectal mass or thigh pain.
Spigelian is an anterior abdominal wall lump.

steps.x: **B. Obturator hernia.** Rule: tender mass per rectum = obturator.

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has a soft lump in his right groin that has grown over 2 months and extends towards the scrotum. It reduces when he lies down. The examiner reduces it and presses over the deep inguinal ring, then asks him to stand and cough to type the hernia.
practice.q: Which finding on examination would confirm an indirect inguinal hernia?
o: Lump below and lateral to the pubic tubercle
